name: Character Voice and Dialogue
title: Character Voice and Dialogue
answer: Character voice and dialogue is the craft of making each speaker on the page sound like a specific person, through word choice, rhythm, vocabulary, what they avoid saying, and how they answer other people. It sits inside literary arts and narrative design alongside plot, point of view, and scene construction. The work covers prose fiction, screenplays, stage plays, game scripts, and branching interactive narrative. The aim is recognisability, so that a reader can tell who is speaking with the attributions removed.

sections.body: Character voice and dialogue is the craft of making each speaker on the page sound like a specific person, through word choice, rhythm, vocabulary, what they avoid saying, and how they answer other people. It sits inside literary arts and narrative design alongside plot, point of view, and scene construction. The work covers prose fiction, screenplays, stage plays, game scripts, and branching interactive narrative. The aim is recognisability, so that a reader can tell who is speaking with the attributions removed.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The everyday kit is a draft in a word processor or screenwriting program, plus character notes, a style sheet, and repeated revision passes. In games and interactive work, dialogue usually lives in a branching script format or a node based editor such as Ink or Twine, and it may later be recorded by voice actors. AI enters as a drafting aid, a line variation generator, or a text to speech step, and the site tracks 2000 audio models that can render written lines as spoken performance. None of that replaces the writer's ear, but it changes how quickly variants can be heard and compared.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A writer builds a character's speech from background, region, era, profession, and temperament, then tests it in scenes against other characters. Common techniques include reading dialogue aloud, cutting attributions to check whether voices are distinct, keeping a phrase list for each character, and revising for subtext so that people rarely say exactly what they mean. AI tools can generate alternate phrasings, simulate a character's replies, or flag lines that read too similarly across a cast. The judgement stays with the writer, because a model tends to produce fluent, averaged speech rather than a voice shaped by a particular life.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Dialogue written by a person is that person's copyright, while text produced by a model raises questions about training data and ownership that are still being tested. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits across AI, and the outcomes will shape what studios and publishers accept in a manuscript or a game script. Practical risks include unintentional similarity to a known character's catchphrases, the use of a living performer's voice without consent, and disclosure clauses in publishing and game contracts. Studios and publishers commonly ask for drafts, prompts, and revision history to show where the words came from.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more hybrid workflows where a writer drafts, a model produces variants, and a voice model performs them for a table read or a prototype. Interactive narrative and games will push further into characters that respond in real time, which raises the bar for keeping a voice consistent across many possible lines. Evaluation is likely to stay human, since distinctiveness is judged by readers and players rather than by a metric. The craft question does not change: whether a character sounds like someone who could exist, and whether the dialogue earns the scene it sits in.
